<action type="say">
Understood—this is a plumbing emergency and you need someone right away.

First, a couple of quick steps to reduce damage (if you haven’t already):
- Turn off the water to the toilet: look for the small shutoff valve on the wall/floor behind the toilet and turn it clockwise until it stops.
- Unplug or move anything electrical on the wet floor and avoid standing water if there are outlets nearby.
- Put down towels or a bucket where water is spreading to keep it from reaching other rooms.

I can get an emergency plumber to you ASAP. I need a few details:
1. Full address (or at least your city + ZIP/postal code):
2. How urgent is this? (Right now within the next few hours, or later today?)
3. Any constraints on who we book? (e.g., “must be highly rated,” “budget-sensitive,” or “earliest available no matter what”)
4. Do you want me to:
   - A) Show you the best few emergency plumbers so you can choose, or
   - B) Book the fastest available option for you automatically?

Once you share this, I’ll search emergency plumbers near you and move to get someone scheduled immediately.</action>

I tried to find an emergency plumber for that address but there are no providers available through this system right now. I can’t place an automatic booking for you, so the fastest path is to contact a local 24/7 plumber directly while we stabilize things.

Immediate steps (only if it’s safe—avoid standing water near electrical outlets):

1. Stop the water:
   - Locate the small shutoff valve behind or beside the toilet (near the floor).
   - Turn it clockwise until it stops. If there’s no valve or it’s stuck, shut off the main water supply to your home if you know where it is.

2. Prevent more damage:
   - Move rugs, boxes, electronics, and anything absorbent or valuable out of the wet area.
   - Use towels, a mop, or a wet/dry vac (if you have one) to remove as much water as possible.
   - If water may get through the floor (upper level), put buckets/pans under any active drips below.

3. Sanitize:
   - After you get the bulk of the water up, use a disinfectant cleaner or a bleach solution (if safe for your flooring) on the affected area, since toilet water can be contaminated.

To get a plumber ASAP, I recommend:
- Searching “24 hour emergency plumber Austin 78701” on your phone and calling the top 2–3 results that:
  - Have good ratings and
  - Explicitly say “24/7” or “emergency service.”
- If you’re in an apartment/office building, call building management or maintenance—they often have an on-call plumber.
- If you have a home warranty or membership (e.g., with a utility or insurer), check their app/website for emergency plumbing dispatch.

If you’d like, tell me what you see when you search (a couple of company names and their quoted arrival times), and I can help you decide which to pick and what to ask them on the phone (e.g., questions about fees, ETA, and cleanup responsibility).</action>

<plan>

</plan>
<action type="say">
You’ve done the right first steps. In an office building, this is usually a building/facilities issue, not something you personally hire a plumber for.

Here’s what to do next, in order:

1) Internal facilities / office contact
- If your company has:
  - Facilities team, office manager, front desk, or a helpdesk system → contact them first.
- What to say (or put in the ticket):
  “We just had a toilet overflow in [floor + room/restroom location]. The water is shut off and we’ve put towels down, but there’s water on the floor. Please contact building maintenance/janitorial ASAP.”

2) Building management / property office
If you can see a building contact number (lobby sign, elevator notice, restroom sign, or in your lease/welcome packet), call them:
- Script:
  “Hi, this is [Your Name] from [Company] in suite [#] on floor [#]. A toilet overflowed in our restroom. We’ve closed the valve and put towels down, but there’s water on the floor. Could you please send building maintenance or janitorial right away to inspect and clean up?”

3) If you’re in a coworking/flex space (WeWork, Regus, etc.)
- Go directly to the community/front desk or call them.
- Same message as above, plus which restroom (e.g., “women’s restroom near conference rooms”).

While you’re waiting:
- Put up a simple sign on the door (“Do not use – plumbing issue”) and keep people out.
- Keep checking nearby areas to make sure water isn’t spreading farther.

If you tell me:
- Whether you’re in a traditional leased suite vs coworking, and
- Whether you already have a building or office manager contact,

I can draft a very short email/Slack message or a phone script tailored exactly to your situation that you can send or read word-for-word.</action>

Here’s exactly what you can use.

1) Email to building management

Subject: Urgent plumbing issue – toilet overflow in [Floor/Suite #]

Hi [Building Management Team],

We just had a toilet overflow in our office restroom and water reached the surrounding floor.

Details:
- Location: [Floor #], Suite [#], [men’s/women’s/unisex] restroom  
- Status: We have shut off the toilet water valve and placed towels to contain the water. The leak has stopped, but the floor is still wet.

Could you please:
1) Send building maintenance to inspect the plumbing, and  
2) Arrange janitorial/cleanup to properly dry and sanitize the area?

This is time-sensitive to avoid damage and odor, so any help as soon as possible would be appreciated.

Thank you,  
[Your Name]  
[Company Name]  
[Phone extension or mobile]

(You can copy/paste this and fill in floor, suite, restroom type, and your info.)

2) Script for calling the building front desk

“Hi, this is [Your Name] from [Company] in suite [#] on floor [#].  
We just had a toilet overflow in our [men’s/women’s/unisex] restroom. We’ve turned off the water at the valve and put towels down, so the water has stopped, but the floor is still wet.

Could you please send building maintenance and janitorial to clean and inspect it as soon as possible? I want to make sure there’s no water damage or sanitation issue.

If you need to reach me, I’m at [your extension/mobile].”

3) When you’re on the phone, quickly confirm:
- “Will your janitorial team handle full cleanup and disinfection, or do we need to do anything else?”  
- “Will maintenance let us know when it’s safe to use that restroom again?”

If you’d like, tell me your floor, suite, and restroom type and I’ll return a fully filled-in email you can paste and send as-is.</action>
